pyharp solves many atmospheric columns, wavelengths and bands in one call, and it can do so on an NVIDIA GPU. This
chapter states what that buys and what it does not. A batched call must give the same fluxes as a loop over single
columns, and a CUDA call the same fluxes as a CPU call, up to round-off. Both claims are measured here for each
solver and each precision. The DISORT solver comes from the separate package pydisort, so its CUDA support depends
on the pydisort version installed next to pyharp; the chapter measures the two versions a user meets, and it
shows what happens when pyharp and pydisort are built against different versions.

::: {.cell execution_count=1}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1}

## Toon on many columns and on CUDA (device and precision of the inputs) {#sec-ch09-toon}

### Summary

pyharp's Toon solver takes the optical properties of many wavelengths and columns in one tensor and returns the
fluxes of all of them. Each column is solved by the same function, independently of the others, on the CPU or on a
CUDA device, whichever holds the input tensors. A user can therefore batch columns freely and move the work to a
GPU without changing the answer: batched and single-column calls agree bit for bit in double precision, and CUDA
agrees with the CPU to $4\times10^{-14}$. In single precision the CUDA and CPU results differ by as much as single
precision itself is from double precision.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** One call solves every (wavelength, column) pair; agreement measure @eq-ch09-toon-nd.

**Data.** Properties (nwave, ncol, nlyr, 3); fluxes (nwave, ncol, nlyr + 1, 4); float32 or float64.

**Placement.** Inside `ToonMcKay89Impl::forward`, after the inputs are checked.

**Activation.** Always; the device and precision of the inputs decide. Default CPU.

**Guarantee / limits.** Batch = loop to $10^{-14}$; CUDA = CPU to $10^{-12}$ (float64).

**Evidence.** See the Tests layer below.
:::

Local symbols: $\mathrm{nd}(a, b)$ the normalised largest difference of two flux arrays [-]; $\epsilon_{32}$ the
single-precision floor of a solver [-].

### Derivation

**The quantity compared.** For two arrays of fluxes $a$ and $b$ of the same shape, over every wavelength, column,
level and channel,

$$
\mathrm{nd}(a, b) = \frac{\max |a - b|}{\max |b|} .
$$ {#eq-ch09-toon-nd}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch09-toon-nd check_ch09_batch_device.py [C1] -->

**Why a batch equals a loop over columns.** Three facts of the code at the pin, in order:

1. `ToonMcKay89Impl::forward` builds one tensor iterator whose elements are the (wavelength, column) pairs: it
   declares the level and channel dimensions of the output static and squashes them, so each element carries a
   whole column ({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89.cpp ToonMcKay89Impl::forward repo=pyharp >}}).
2. The CPU driver `call_toon89_sw_cpu` calls the shortwave kernel once per element with its own scratch buffer
   ({{< code src/rtsolver/rtsolver_dispatch.cpp call_toon89_sw_cpu repo=pyharp >}}); the kernel reads only that
   column's properties and boundary values ({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_shortwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_shortwave repo=pyharp >}}).
3. No step sums or compares across elements, so the order in which threads visit the elements cannot change a
   result.

A batched call therefore executes, for each column, the same floating-point operations as a call with that column
alone, and @eq-ch09-toon-nd between the two is zero. The thermal path adds one step before the kernel: the band
Planck radiance of every level is computed by a tensor expression over all levels of the call. Its result can
differ in the last bit when the tensor's shape changes, if torch evaluates the expression with a different
vectorised path; that is a hypothesis for the measured $3.5\times10^{-16}$, not a measured cause.

**Why CUDA differs from the CPU only by round-off.** The CUDA driver `call_toon89_sw_cuda` runs the same kernel
template, one thread per element, with its scratch interleaved across threads
({{< code src/rtsolver/rtsolver_dispatch.cu call_toon89_sw_cuda repo=pyharp >}},
{{< code src/loops.cuh repo=pyharp >}}). What can differ is the arithmetic below
the kernel's source: the CUDA compiler contracts `a*b + c` into one fused multiply-add, and the device's `exp` and
`sqrt` round differently from the host's. Each such difference is a rounding of the last place, $\epsilon_{\mathrm{mach}}/2$
relative, amplified by the condition of the tridiagonal solve. For a tolerance this gives $10^{-12}$ in double
precision: a thousand times the $\epsilon_{\mathrm{mach}} = 2.2\times10^{-16}$ of one rounding.

**Single precision.** A float32 result is itself $\epsilon_{32} = \mathrm{nd}(F_{32}, F_{64})$ away from the
float64 result of the same device. Two float32 results on two devices can be held to

$$
\mathrm{nd}(F^{\mathrm{CUDA}}_{32}, F^{\mathrm{CPU}}_{32}) \le \max\bigl(10^{-5},\, 2\,\epsilon_{32}\bigr) ,
$$ {#eq-ch09-toon-tol32}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch09-toon-tol32 check_ch09_batch_device.py [C8] -->

no closer: each may be off by $\epsilon_{32}$ in opposite directions.

What is exact and what is approximate: the equality of batch and loop is exact for the shortwave kernel by the
three facts above; the CUDA-CPU difference is round-off, bounded but not zero. The check is
`check_ch09_batch_device.py` (Tests layer).

### Numerical method

The inputs are 3 wavelengths (500-1000, 1000-1500 and 1500-2000 $\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$) $\times$ 64 columns $\times$
40 layers, with layer optical depths log-uniform between $10^{-3}$ and $10^{0.5}$, single-scattering albedos
between 0 and 0.99, asymmetry parameters between 0 and 0.85, $\mu_0$ between 0.1 and 1, surface albedos between 0
and 0.5, beam fluxes between 0.5 and 2, and level temperatures from 300 K at the bottom to 180 K at the top with
$\pm 5$ K noise (seed 1). The thermal runs use the flags `planck,hard_surface`. Each comparison is made in float64
and in float32: the whole batch against 64 single-column calls and against 3 single-wavelength calls on the CPU,
CUDA against CPU, and on CUDA the batch against 8 single-column calls.

@fig-ch09-toon-device shows the measured differences. A user moves a Toon call to the GPU by moving its inputs; the
module holds no tensors:

```python
toon = pyharp.ToonMcKay89(op)                       # no buffers to move
prop = prop.to("cuda")                              # (nwave, ncol, nlyr, 3)
flux = toon(prop, fbeam=fbeam.to("cuda"), umu0=umu0.to("cuda"),
            albedo=albedo.to("cuda"))
```

| CPU driver, shortwave | {{< code src/rtsolver/rtsolver_dispatch.cpp call_toon89_sw_cpu repo=pyharp >}} | `call_toon89_sw_cpu` | CPU inputs |

: Code map of Toon batching and dispatch. {#tbl-ch09-toon-code}

1. `ToonMcKay89Impl::forward` checks the shapes of `umu0`, `fbeam` and `albedo`, makes the properties contiguous,
   and builds the iterator; every input must share the device and the precision of the properties
   ({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89.cpp ToonMcKay89Impl::forward repo=pyharp >}}).
2. The dispatch stub selects `call_toon89_sw_cpu` or `call_toon89_sw_cuda` from the device type; the thermal pair is
   `call_toon89_lw_cpu` ({{< code src/rtsolver/rtsolver_dispatch.cpp call_toon89_lw_cpu repo=pyharp >}}) and its
   CUDA twin.
3. On the CPU the elements are split into chunks of one per thread; on CUDA each thread takes one element and a
   slice of the scratch block ({{< code src/loops.cuh repo=pyharp >}}).

On the CPU, the batched shortwave fluxes equal the single-column and single-wavelength loops bit for bit in float64
and float32. The thermal batch equals the single-wavelength loop bit for bit and the single-column loop to
$3.5\times10^{-16}$ (float64) and $2.5\times10^{-7}$ (float32). On CUDA, $\mathrm{nd}$ against the CPU is
$4.2\times10^{-14}$ (shortwave) and $1.7\times10^{-14}$ (thermal) in float64, and the CUDA batch equals 8
single-column CUDA calls bit for bit. In float32 the CUDA-CPU difference is $1.4\times10^{-5}$ (shortwave) and
$1.2\times10^{-5}$ (thermal), against float32 floors $\epsilon_{32}$ of $1.3\times10^{-5}$ and
$8.5\times10^{-6}$: within @eq-ch09-toon-tol32. No Toon operation is unsupported on CUDA.[^ch09-toon-run]

pyharp's `test_toon.release` runs nine cases on CPU and CUDA in both precisions; in the CUDA build all 39 tests
pass, the 18 CUDA instances included.[^ch09-toon-ctest] Every measurement here is the same under pydisort 1.7.1
and 1.8.13, as Toon does not use pydisort.

### Limits

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
- **A float32 tolerance must be read against the float32 floor.** CUDA and CPU float32 results differ by about
  $10^{-5}$, the same as float32 from float64; a tolerance below that will fail on correct code.
- **Not measured.** Batches above 192 columns per call, layer counts other than 40, the `zenith_correction` flag on
  CUDA, timing on CUDA, and GPUs other than the one of the footnote.
- **Mixed devices.** Inputs on different devices are refused by torch when the iterator is built; this report does
  not measure the error messages.
:::

### Summary

When a band runs with `solver: disort`, pyharp hands the column to pydisort, so whether DISORT can run on a GPU is
decided by the pydisort installed next to pyharp, not by pyharp. Two versions matter: 1.7.1, the version pyharp's
CI installs, and 1.8.13, the version `pip` installs for pyharp's requirement `pydisort>=1.7.1`. With 1.7.1 DISORT
cannot run on CUDA at all: the call raises. With 1.8.13 it runs and agrees with the CPU to round-off at 4, 16 and
32 streams, but not at 8 streams, and not to round-off for thermal columns with a single-scattering albedo of
one. On the CPU the two versions give bit-identical fluxes, and batching is exact in both.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** Which DISORT operations run on CUDA, per pydisort version, and how close they come to the CPU.

**Data.** Properties (nwave, ncol, nlyr, 2 + nmom); fluxes (nwave, ncol, nlyr + 1, 2).

**Placement.** Inside `DisortImpl::forward`, called by `RadiationBandImpl::forward`.

**Activation.** `solver: disort`; device and precision of the inputs. Default CPU.

**Guarantee / limits.** 1.7.1: no CUDA. 1.8.13: round-off except at `nstr` 8 and thermal $\omega = 1$.

**Evidence.** See the Tests layer below.
:::

Local symbols: $\mathrm{nd}$ as in @eq-ch09-toon-nd; $\delta\omega_{\mathrm{D}}$ the margin cdisort subtracts from a
single-scattering albedo of one [-].

### Derivation

**Why a DISORT batch equals a loop over columns.** pydisort keeps one cdisort state per (wavelength, column) pair and
runs the column solver `c_disort` once per element of a tensor iterator, with no step across elements:
`DisortImpl::forward` builds the iterator ({{< code src/disort.cpp DisortImpl::forward repo=pydisort >}}) and the
CPU driver `call_disort_cpu` loops over its elements ({{< code src/disort_dispatch.cpp call_disort_cpu repo=pydisort >}}).
The argument is that of @sec-ch09-toon, Derivation, and gives $\mathrm{nd} = 0$ between a batch and a loop.

**Why columns with $\omega = 1$ need a looser tolerance.** cdisort does not solve a conservative layer as such; it
moves the single-scattering albedo off one,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\delta\omega_{\mathrm{D}} &= 100\,\epsilon_{\mathrm{mach}} \\
\omega &\leftarrow 1 - \delta\omega_{\mathrm{D}} ,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch09-disort-dither}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch09-disort-dither check_ch09_batch_device.py -->
<!-- equation-source: eq-ch09-disort-dither cdisort's treatment of a single-scattering albedo of one -->

with $\epsilon_{\mathrm{mach}}$ the double-precision machine epsilon. @eq-ch09-disort-dither is applied in `c_disort`
({{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_disort repo=pydisort >}}). Near $\omega = 1$ the solution changes fast with
$\omega$: the eigenvalues of the homogeneous solution approach zero, so the round-off of the two devices is amplified
far more than for $\omega < 1$. The comparison therefore holds those columns to $10^{-9}$ in float64, and the others
to the $10^{-12}$ of @sec-ch09-toon.

**What decides CUDA support.** A call on CUDA tensors reaches pydisort's dispatch stub, which has a CUDA entry only
if the installed pydisort library contains one. At the pydisort pin the CUDA driver `call_disort_cuda` is
registered in the source, but the line that would call the column solver is commented out
({{< code src/disort_dispatch.cu call_disort_cuda repo=pydisort >}}); the 1.7.1 wheel ships no CUDA library at
all. A source build of that version with CUDA would therefore return fluxes the kernel never wrote; that is read
from the code, not measured.

What is exact and what is approximate: batch against loop is exact; CUDA against CPU is round-off where the two
devices run the same solver. The check is `check_ch09_batch_device.py` (Tests layer).

### Numerical method

The inputs are 3 wavelengths $\times$ 32 columns $\times$ 20 layers, drawn as in @sec-ch09-toon, with the
single-scattering albedo set to one in every layer of columns 0 to 3. Each comparison runs at 4, 8, 16 and 32
streams with Henyey-Greenstein moments $\chi_l = g^l$, shortwave (flags `lamber,quiet,onlyfl`) and thermal (adding
`planck`), in float64 and float32. The DISORT object is configured by `disort_config`
({{< code python/disort.py disort_config repo=pyharp >}}). The same comparison is made for DISORT inside a
`RadiationBand`, built from `tests/rayleigh_test.yaml` with 8 streams and 4 columns and moved with `.cuda()`; the
band clamps $\omega$ to $1 - 10^{-12}$ before the solver ({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}}).

### Code

@tbl-ch09-disort-code lists the code at the pydisort pin that decides batching and CUDA support.

| what | code link | symbol | switch |
|---|---|---|---|
| iterator over (wavelength, column) | {{< code src/disort.cpp DisortImpl::forward repo=pydisort >}} | `DisortImpl::forward` | `solver: disort` |
| CPU driver | {{< code src/disort_dispatch.cpp call_disort_cpu repo=pydisort >}} | `call_disort_cpu` | CPU inputs |
| CUDA driver (body commented out) | {{< code src/disort_dispatch.cu call_disort_cuda repo=pydisort >}} | `call_disort_cuda` | CUDA inputs |

: Code map of DISORT batching and dispatch. {#tbl-ch09-disort-code}

1. `RadiationBandImpl::forward` assembles the properties, clamps $\omega \le 1 - \delta\omega$ with
   $\delta\omega = 10^{-12}$ (float64) or $10^{-6}$ (float32), and calls the band's solver
   ({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}}).
2. `DisortImpl::forward` checks the shapes against the configured wave and column counts and builds the iterator
   ({{< code src/disort.cpp DisortImpl::forward repo=pydisort >}}).
3. The dispatch stub picks `call_disort_cpu`, or on CUDA tensors `call_disort_cuda` if the installed library has it;
   otherwise torch raises `DispatchStub: missing kernel for cuda`.

Under pydisort 1.7.1 the check prints 72 lines with no failure: every DISORT and band call on CUDA is reported
`UNSUPPORTED` with the message `DispatchStub: missing kernel for cuda`, and every CPU comparison
passes.[^ch09-disort-171] Under pydisort 1.8.13 it prints 88 lines with no failure and 10 lines marked
`EXPECTED-FAIL`: the candidate defects of the Limits layer.[^ch09-disort-1813] On the CPU, DISORT gives
bit-identical fluxes under the two versions on the grid of the solver-comparison chapter, @sec-ch05.

### Limits

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
- **No DISORT on CUDA with pydisort 1.7.1.** A band with `solver: disort` on CUDA tensors raises
  `DispatchStub: missing kernel for cuda`. pyharp's CI installs exactly this version.
- **Candidate defect: pydisort 1.8.13 on CUDA at 8 streams.** At `nstr` 8, CUDA differs from the CPU by
  $8.3\times10^{-5}$ (shortwave) and $2.9\times10^{-6}$ (thermal) in float64; in float32 the $\omega = 1$ columns
  are wrong by $6.2\times10^{4}$ and $5.8\times10^{8}$ times the largest flux, while staying finite. In version 1.8.13
  pydisort solves 4- and 8-stream flux-only problems on CUDA by a reduced "fast flux" path and sends $\omega = 1$
  columns to its general solver; the defect is confined to 8 streams. That version is not the pin of this report,
  so its code is described here and not cited; the measurement is the evidence.[^ch09-disort-1813]
- **Candidate defect: thermal $\omega = 1$ columns on CUDA, pydisort 1.8.13.** In float64 they differ from the CPU
  by $7\times10^{-8}$ to $1.1\times10^{-7}$ at every stream count, against $1.6\times10^{-13}$ for the other
  columns of the same runs. The cause is not measured.
- Both are one run on one GPU; they stay candidates until a second, independent run agrees.
- **Not measured.** Stream counts above 32 on CUDA, intensities (`onlyfl` off), timing on CUDA, and other GPUs.
:::

## Building pyharp against pydisort and CUDA (`-DCUDA=ON`, `pydisort>=1.7.1`) {#sec-ch09-build}

### Summary

pyharp is compiled against pydisort: its C++ library includes pydisort's headers, creates pydisort's objects, and
loads pydisort's shared library at run time. The two must therefore come from the same pydisort version. pyharp's
package metadata asks only for `pydisort>=1.7.1`, so a later `pip install` can replace pydisort under an existing
pyharp build. This section measures what then happens. When pyharp is built against pydisort 1.7.1 and run with
1.8.13, the test that builds a DISORT band passes its assertions and the process then aborts with
`double free or corruption`: the defect-register item D1. Builds that match their pydisort never abort. The
section also records one build failure of the CUDA option.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** The build contract between pyharp and pydisort, and what breaking it does (D1).

**Data.** pyharp's `libharp_release.so`; the pydisort headers and library it was built and run with.

**Placement.** At build time (`cmake`, `pip install`) and when Python loads pyharp.

**Activation.** `-DCUDA=ON` (default off); the installed pydisort, required `>=1.7.1`.

**Guarantee / limits.** Run with the pydisort pyharp was built against; other pairs are undefined.

**Evidence.** See the Tests layer below.
:::

D1 is an item of the report's defect register and stays a candidate until a second, independent run agrees.

### Derivation

No equation describes this section; the argument is a chain of code facts, each measured or read at the pin.

1. *pyharp loads one pydisort library, by an absolute path.* pyharp's library `libharp_release.so` needs
   `libdisort_release.so`, and the build gives it an absolute search path into the pydisort installation found by
   CMake ({{< code cmake/modules/FindDisort.cmake repo=pyharp >}}). The Python extension adds a relative path to the
   pydisort next to it (`extra_link_args` in {{< code setup.py repo=pyharp >}}). Measured on an installed build:
   the library's only search entries are absolute, ending in `pydisort/lib` and `torch/lib` (`check_ch09_abi.py`
   [C5]). If pydisort is reinstalled in the same environment, the same path then holds the new library.
2. *pyharp allocates pydisort's objects with the sizes it was compiled with.* `RadiationBandImpl::reset` creates the
   solver as `disort::Disort(options->disort())` ({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandImpl::reset repo=pyharp >}}),
   and `create_disort_config` creates the options object
   ({{< code src/radiation/disort_config.cpp create_disort_config repo=pyharp >}}). Both allocations are compiled
   into pyharp from pydisort's headers; the constructors that fill the objects run in the loaded pydisort library.
3. *The two versions lay these objects out differently.* Compiled against each version's headers, `disort_state`,
   `DisortImpl` and `DisortOptionsImpl` are 1336, 488 and 1576 bytes with pydisort 1.7.1 and 1344, 496 and 1584
   bytes with 1.8.13 (`check_ch09_abi.py` [C1]-[C3]). Version 1.8.13 adds one field to the cdisort state and one
   member to `DisortImpl`, which is consistent with the 8-byte growth.
4. *So a 1.7.1 build run with 1.8.13 writes past its allocations.* The 1.8.13 constructor fills a 496-byte layout
   into a 488-byte block, and the heap is corrupted. The allocator notices when the block is freed, which for the
   module object is at interpreter exit, after the tests have passed. Steps 1 to 3 are measured or read from the
   code; that this overwrite is the one the allocator reports is consistent with the measured abort and was not
   traced further.
5. *The reverse pairing has the opposite error.* A 1.8.13 build run with 1.7.1 allocates 8 bytes more than the
   library writes. Nothing aborts, but pyharp then reads fields the library never set; the behaviour is undefined
   and no test detects it.

**The CUDA build on a 12.x toolkit.** `CMakeLists.txt` adds the architectures 90 and 120 to its list whenever the
CUDA toolkit is 12.0 or newer (`_cuda_arch_list`, {{< code CMakeLists.txt repo=pyharp >}}). nvcc 12.6
rejects architecture 120 (`nvcc fatal: Unsupported gpu architecture 'compute_120'`), so `-DCUDA=ON` fails at the
pin with that toolkit. The builds measured in this chapter move that one condition to 12.8 with the patch
`derivation-checks/ch09_setup/cuda-arch-sm120.patch`, which `derivation-checks/ch09_setup.sh` applies when nvcc
is older than 12.8; the patch touches only the list of CUDA architectures, not any code.

### Numerical method

The measurement uses four environments, each built by one call of `derivation-checks/ch09_setup.sh` (the four
calls are listed in `derivation-checks/ch09_run.sh`): pyharp at the pin with `-DCUDA=ON`, torch 2.10.0+cu126, and
pydisort installed from its published wheels, checked by hash:

1. built against 1.7.1, run with 1.7.1;
2. built against 1.8.13, run with 1.8.13;
3. built against 1.7.1, then pydisort reinstalled in place as 1.8.13 (`pip install --no-deps --force-reinstall`);
4. built against 1.8.13, then reinstalled in place as 1.7.1.

In each, pyharp's `tests/test_rayleigh.py` and then the whole Python test suite run three times, and the exit status
and any heap-corruption message are recorded. The type sizes are measured by compiling a ten-line program against
each version's headers.

: Code map of the pyharp-pydisort build contract. {#tbl-ch09-build-code}

1. `FindDisort.cmake` asks the active Python for the installed pydisort and takes its header and library
   directories from there ({{< code cmake/modules/FindDisort.cmake repo=pyharp >}}); the version is printed at
   configure time and not recorded in the build.
2. `setup.py` links the extension against the libraries of the CMake build and adds the search path
   `$ORIGIN/../pydisort/lib` ({{< code setup.py repo=pyharp >}}).
3. `pyproject.toml` requires `pydisort>=1.7.1` both to build and to run ({{< code pyproject.toml repo=pyharp >}}).

### Tests

@tbl-ch09-build-tests lists the checks.

| test (ctest name) | what it asserts | tolerance | where the tolerance comes from |
|---|---|---|---|
| `check_ch09_d1.sh` | no heap-corruption abort in matched builds | none allowed | D1 is the abort |
| `check_ch09_d1.sh` | the abort in a drifted build is reported, not hidden | `EXPECTED-FAIL` | D1, candidate |
| `check_ch09_abi.py` | type sizes per pydisort version; pyharp's search path | reported | a measurement |
| `test_rayleigh.py` (pytest) | the Rayleigh band with DISORT returns finite fluxes | as in the test | set in the test |

: Tests of the build contract. {#tbl-ch09-build-tests}

In the two matched environments, `test_rayleigh.py` passes 3 times out of 3 and the full suite finishes 3 times
out of 3 without an abort. Built against 1.7.1 and run with 1.8.13, `test_rayleigh.py` reports its 2 tests passed
and then aborts with `double free or corruption (!prev)` and exit status 134, 3 times out of 3. The full suite
aborts too, 3 times out of 3, with `corrupted size vs. prev_size` or `free(): invalid pointer`; the check also
counts an exit by segmentation fault (status 139) as a crash. Built against
1.8.13 and run with 1.7.1, nothing aborts in 6 runs.[^ch09-build-d1] The abort comes from the DISORT test of
`test_rayleigh.py`, `test_radiation_band_regularizes_conservative_ssa_for_disort`: run alone it aborts, and the
other test of the file does not.[^ch09-build-iso]

In every environment the full suite also reports 10 to 12 failures in the spectroscopy tests and the Sonora test.
They are the same in all four environments, and none involves DISORT: a download that returns HTTP error 500, a
missing data file, and test code that calls functions the package at the pin does not have.

### Limits

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
- **D1 (candidate): pyharp built against pydisort 1.7.1 and run with 1.8.13 aborts** after a DISORT band is created,
  at the latest at exit. Running with the pydisort pyharp was built against avoids it in every measured run.
- **The reverse pairing is silent**, not safe: no abort, but pyharp reads object fields the library did not write.
- **`-DCUDA=ON` fails with CUDA 12.6** at the pin, because the architecture list includes 120. Only 12.6 was
  measured.
- **One host, one GPU, published wheels.** pydisort was not built from source; the wheels are identified by
  version and file hash in the footnote.
:::
